name: Bianca Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government, and we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so you can separate what you'd say in public from what you really think. What does a working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the showtimes team for a large cinema chain's regional office. Four schedulers work out which film plays on which screen, book school groups and answer managers when a projector goes down and the evening must be rearranged. I've managed the team for seven years and do a sound enough job, though I still ask a colleague to check the trickier licence dates. I have a bachelor's degree and use the phone and booking system, not AI; I've never tried an AI tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters about that work, and what is pressing at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding a screen for a school group so the children don't come back disappointed. I'm 43, married to Owen, who prepares bread at a bakery on a shift rota; our daughter is sixteen and our son is eight. We have a mortgage and barely two weeks of expenses saved since the car repair. My pay is at the lower end for managers and there are few cinema offices nearby. I don't need a new gadget to know a cancelled show makes a parent angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our booking system might file group requests faster, but the screens and phone calls would still be mine. Cinema attendance has been soft this year, though. AI turning out quiet wouldn't bring back the Friday crowds or repair our car bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my schedulers to keep checking the cinema manager's screen report before moving a show. I'd tell Owen the new filing shortcut won't change the job much. I wouldn't start posting about a tool I've never used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the team would probably stay, but our mortgage still worries me. Two weeks of savings won't cover a bad month if Owen loses bakery shifts, and a cinema can cut office hours when ticket sales dip. I know how to do this work, but there are few other places to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next week I'd check each Friday screen list with the cinema manager by phone before we print the posters. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep the rota, stop buying snacks at work for six weeks and put the saved 10 a week toward a one-month cash cushion. If Owen's rota shrinks, we'd pay mortgage and food first and pause that saving rather than borrow to make it look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our bills, even though the booking work stays familiar. The quiet card doesn't buy us a month's safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How bad was the last Friday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We planned three evening shows and filled half of two rooms. The manager sent a photo of empty seats because my spreadsheet made the night look stronger. I can't pay the mortgage with a coloured spreadsheet cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children notice the snack cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much; those snacks are mine at work. I'd rather stop that than take money from our son's school trip. The ten a week is small, but it's within my control.

say: I'd tell schedulers to check **screen reports** before moving a show.
I'd tell Owen a filing shortcut leaves most **booking calls** with us.
think: Our **mortgage still worries me** with only two weeks saved.
Soft ticket sales and Owen's variable shifts could cut **household hours** even without major AI.
do: Check each **Friday screen list** by phone before posters print.
Stop **work snacks** for six weeks; save ten weekly only if Owen's rota holds and both wages cover mortgage and food.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills despite familiar work.
S0.quote: I can't pay the mortgage with a coloured spreadsheet cell.
fieldNote: The **empty-seat photo** unsettles her more than modest filing automation.
Two weeks saved and **variable bakery shifts** make even a mild scenario financially anxious.
Her first cut is **her own snacks**, not the children's school trip.

Save ten weekly only if Owen's rota holds and both wages cover mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing show notices, booking groups, planning screens and answering managers are almost all my team's hours. A stronger system could arrange a whole week of showtimes before a projector is even switched on. Someone still needs to open the cinema, but my office isn't the person opening it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chain should give a real headcount and notice before taking away hours. I'd tell my team to keep the change log so wrong bookings have a name and a date. I wouldn't tell friends that every office post can turn into a floor job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own role could shrink, and Owen's bakery wage won't carry the mortgage by itself. I'm not the most skilled person with a booking system, and I've never used AI, so I won't be fast at the new one. I think the company could keep one scheduler for several cinemas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the director for a written list of jobs that move into software and the dates of any cuts. I'd keep checking the change log with the team while a pilot runs, and ask about a paid duty shift at the cinema foyer only if a manager can cover my current desk. I'd cut our paid television package and keep that money for the car repair balance while the headcount is unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my wage and the people beside me. I don't want to learn about a cut from a new rota on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the scheduling system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the senior scheduler run it on last month's show list, but I would not take a live week first. I have never used an AI tool and won't tell my team I have. If it proves reliable and the firm pays for instruction, I could learn, but I won't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company won't give a headcount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking and put my own applications in at the few nearby venues. An advert would have to name the pay before I took time off to interview. Owen and I can't gamble the mortgage on a rumour.

feel: I feel **anxious** about my wage and my schedulers' hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a full thinking system could plan all our screens, settle a film licence and answer a school group. The ushers still check rooms and clean seats until robots arrive around 2031, but I don't get those shifts just because I know the timetable. My office wage could vanish first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the schedulers the 2028 date plainly and ask for written notice and paid openings. I'd tell Owen we need his bakery rota on the table, not hopes of extra shifts. In public I'd say firms may change, but they should pay for apprenticeships when they need new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my office job to go in 2028, and two weeks of savings won't meet a whole month of mortgage, food and children's costs. Owen's confirmed bakery shifts cover some bills, not all. I lie awake thinking about how to tell our ten-year-old that the house might have to be sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop the planned kitchen cabinets before paying the deposit and keep that cash for the mortgage. I'd ask the nearest cinema manager whether a paid usher and safety-check post is actually open, what it pays and whether someone would train me on the floor. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my wage ends, I'd apply only if its wage with Owen's confirmed hours covers mortgage, food and child care; I'd ask my sister whether she could handle after-school pickup and rely on it only if she agrees; otherwise I'd keep searching while we speak to the lender before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can make phone calls, but I can't make two weeks of cash last a season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an usher post really be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical cleaning and fire-exit checks may last until robots around 2031. The rota and ticket questions could be automated in 2028, so I'd need paid floor duties rather than a new name for booking. I have no offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the children about the cabinets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the old kitchen will do for now. Our daughter is nearly grown and can understand the numbers; our son shouldn't have to carry our mortgage fear. A new cupboard is not worth another sleepless night.

I'd tell Owen we must count **confirmed bakery shifts**, not hoped-for hours.
think: I expect my **office wage to vanish** in 2028.
Two weeks saved and Owen's shifts cannot cover **family bills** for long.
do: Stop the **kitchen-cabinet deposit** and keep the money for mortgage.
Check for **open paid floor work** with training; ask my sister about pickup before relying on her agreement.
**Apply** only if confirmed wages cover mortgage, food and childcare; otherwise keep searching and call lender before missing payments.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about the mortgage and the short cash runway.
S2.quote: A new cupboard is not worth another sleepless night.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 office loss** while physical usher duties face robots around 2031.
A move requires **an open paid post**, training, enough wages and agreed school pickup.
She postpones **kitchen cabinets** while protecting the children from premature mortgage fear.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen cabinets before paying the deposit
Take paid floor job with training only if combined wages cover bills and pickup is agreed
Ask sister about after-school pickup and confirm agreement before accepting any new shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn what paid floor work actually involves before the scheduling desk faces AGI in 2031. Its booking and rota work still changes then, and robots reach the physical cinema floor around 2034. A foyer uniform would not protect my wage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chain to offer paid practice in real floor roles, not just videos about customer service. I'd tell Owen we can cut expenses while we still have two wages. I would not call a cinema-floor title a guaranteed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep a wage if a paid safety-check or foyer post opens, but I don't know whether its lower pay would cover the mortgage. Five years gives me time to ask and train without resigning first. I still worry about my office job because the screens are scheduled by thought, not by hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the cinema manager for a paid shadow shift each month; if approved and my sister agrees to school pickup, I'd complete the floor checks with a trained usher. I'd put 20 weekly toward cash only when our confirmed wages cover mortgage, food and school costs. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted floor role only if its wage with Owen's covers those bills; otherwise I'd keep the scheduling wage through notice while searching the few local employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with a bit more time to find out what the floor wage really is. The mortgage still asks for the full amount each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the fire exit before a school group enters and see who clears a screen when a projector fails. I know the showtime, but not every safety procedure. I'd need someone to show me the route before I signed a check sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with her brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She might, but she will be twenty-one and may not live nearby then. I would ask my sister first and pay for after-school care if the wage allowed it. I won't make the older child my unpaid backup plan.

steps.text: Complete paid monthly floor shadow shifts only with manager approval and agreed school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll be 53, our daughter twenty-six and our son eighteen. The scheduling desk still faces AGI in 2036; physical floor tasks face robots around 2039. I would like to have paid down the mortgage by then, but two weeks saved today does not make that a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to offer apprenticeships on paid time while there are still cinema jobs. I'd tell our children to work hard and pick skills they can use, without me choosing their trade. I would tell other parents to keep the household budget honest before making a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have more cash and floor experience by 2036 if Owen's work stays steady and the cinema funds shifts. I don't expect my booking title to save me when AGI can schedule every screen. A physical post might buy time until 2039, but the pay has to keep the home going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for a paid venue safety course and supervised floor days, and complete them only if the cinema funds the hours and school pickup is arranged. I'd save 30 weekly toward one month of expenses only when confirmed wages cover mortgage, food and school costs, stopping if Owen's bakery shifts fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted physical venue job only if its wage with Owen's covers those bills; otherwise I'd search nearby firms and talk to the lender before an instalment goes late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our income even with ten years. More time helps only if there are paid shifts to practise on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the cinema won't fund the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the scheduling job while it pays and ask another venue about an actual paid opening. I won't spend the mortgage reserve on a course with no post at the end. My husband would remind me work must pay the bills, not just keep me busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children still need your help at those ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect they'll want help sometimes, but they should make their own choices. I would offer a room if we still have one, not direct our daughter's career because I'm worried about mine. Our son may still be finishing school, so I won't count his wages in the budget.

A physical post helps only if its **wage covers our home** before 2039 robots.

fieldNote: Her **resistance to new AI** stays clear; she prefers paid site learning and real wages.
The savings plan is **conditional on bakery shifts**, mortgage and child costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A system that can plan every screen and answer every group could take my office wage before I have money or a paid floor role to move into. Notice, a posted job at a wage that covers our mortgage, and training on paid time would help. My sister might watch our son during a new shift if she agrees, but I cannot book her life for her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the family standing at a locked screen door after their show was moved. My schedule may be perfect on paper, but a parent still has to explain the change to a child. I would rather take the complaint than leave a sign to do all the talking.

headlineQuote: I would rather take the complaint than leave a sign to do all the talking.
portrait: Bianca, **43**, has managed four cinema schedulers for seven years and checks difficult film licences with a colleague.
She has a **bachelor's degree** and average skill, lower manager pay, and has never used AI tools.
She and Owen have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with two weeks saved after a car repair.
She would seek **paid venue work** if office scheduling goes, but childcare, actual openings and affordable wages limit each move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her showtimes wage before she finds a paid venue role.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** and paid training tied to a posted job with wages covering their mortgage.
Childcare from **her sister** only if her sister can agree to the new shifts.
